title: Growing Up in 1955 America: The World That Vanished Forever

scenes.text: If you were born somewhere around nineteen forty-eight, I want you to close your eyes for a moment. It's a cool September morning in nineteen fifty-five. You're seven years old. The screen door slams behind you, and your mother calls out from the kitchen, telling you not to let it slam, the way she has a thousand times before.
scenes.caption: SEPTEMBER 1955

scenes.text: Your shoes are new, a little too stiff, bought one size big so you'll grow into them. And leaning against the porch, red paint shining in the early light, is the thing you have dreamed about all summer long. Your very first bicycle.
scenes.caption: YOUR FIRST BICYCLE

scenes.text: You don't know it yet, but you are standing at the start of a remarkable journey. In the next nine years you'll see rock and roll arrive. You'll see a little silver ball go up into space and frighten the grown-ups. You'll learn to hide under a school desk, learn to dance, and learn to drive. And one day, with money you saved yourself, you'll turn a key in an engine that belongs to you.
scenes.caption: FROM 1955 TO 1964

scenes.text: From your first bicycle, to your first car. This is what it was like to grow up in nineteen fifty-five America. So pour yourself a cup of coffee, get comfortable, and let's go back, one more time.
scenes.caption: GROWING UP IN 1955 AMERICA

scenes.text: Let's start where every day started and ended. At home. If your family was like millions of others in nineteen fifty-five, you might have been living in a brand-new house. After the war, America built homes at a pace it had never seen before. Places like Levittown, out on Long Island, turned potato fields into whole neighborhoods almost overnight.
scenes.caption: LEVITTOWN, LONG ISLAND
scenes.chapter: The house you came home to

scenes.text: The houses looked alike. Two or three bedrooms. One bathroom, which the whole family shared, and which you learned to get in and out of quickly in the morning. A picture window in the front room, so everybody could see the lawn, and the lawn could see everybody. With a G I Bill loan, a young veteran could move his family in with very little money down.
scenes.caption: THE NEW SUBURBS

scenes.text: And the kitchen. That was the heart of it all. Maybe your mother's kitchen was painted a soft turquoise, or butter yellow, or mint green. There was a chrome-edged table with a Formica top, and vinyl chairs that stuck to the backs of your legs in summer. The refrigerator had rounded corners and a handle you had to pull hard.
scenes.caption: MOTHER'S KITCHEN

scenes.text: If your family was doing well, there might be an electric mixer on the counter, and a pressure cooker that hissed and rattled and made you just a little nervous. Monday was wash day. The wringer washer churned in the basement, and the sheets went out on the line in the yard, snapping in the wind and smelling like sunshine when they came back in.
scenes.caption: MONDAY WAS WASH DAY

scenes.text: Dinner was at six o'clock. Not five-thirty. Not whenever you felt like it. Six o'clock. Your father came home, hung up his hat, and the family sat down together. Meatloaf on Monday. Maybe fish sticks on Friday, because those had only just arrived in the grocery freezer a couple of years before.
scenes.caption: DINNER AT SIX O'CLOCK

scenes.text: There was Jell-O salad with something suspended inside it that you were never quite sure about. And you did not leave the table until your plate was clean, because there were children going hungry somewhere in the world, and your mother made sure you knew it.
scenes.caption: CLEAN YOUR PLATE

scenes.text: The milkman came to the house. Think about that. A man in a white uniform brought glass bottles to your back step, and took the empty ones away. The bread man came too, sometimes. And the doctor, if you were sick enough, still made house calls with a black leather bag.
scenes.caption: THE MILKMAN CAME TO YOU

scenes.text: Then there was the television. By the middle of the nineteen fifties, around two out of every three American homes had a set, according to the industry counts of the time. Just a few years earlier, it had been almost nobody. If your family had one, it was a big wooden cabinet with a small, rounded screen, and the picture was black and white.
scenes.caption: TV IN ~2 OF 3 HOMES

scenes.text: Sometimes the picture rolled, and your father would get up and fiddle with the knobs, or climb up on the roof to turn the antenna while somebody inside shouted, better, no, worse, go back. There were only a handful of channels. When the broadcast day ended, late at night, the station played the national anthem.
scenes.caption: ADJUSTING THE ANTENNA

scenes.text: Then the screen turned to a test pattern, humming at you in the dark living room. And you weren't supposed to sit too close to it. Everybody's mother said it would ruin your eyes.
scenes.caption: DON'T SIT SO CLOSE

scenes.text: On Saturday mornings, your mother went to the supermarket, a big bright new kind of store with wide aisles and shopping carts. At the checkout, the cashier handed her little sheets of trading stamps, and at home you licked them and pasted them into booklets at the kitchen table. Enough books, and you could trade them in for a toaster, or a lamp, or a set of dishes. It felt like getting something for free.
scenes.caption: TRADING STAMPS

scenes.text: Now it's eight o'clock in the morning, and you're walking to school. Yes, walking. Most kids walked, or rode their bikes, sometimes a mile or more, and nobody thought twice about it. You walked with your brother, or the kids from down the block. If it was raining, you got wet. If it was snowing, you got a story to tell for the rest of your life.
scenes.caption: WALKING TO SCHOOL

scenes.text: In your hand was your lunchbox. A metal one, if you were lucky, with a picture on the side. A cowboy hero, maybe. And in nineteen fifty-five, quite possibly Davy Crockett, because every kid in America was crazy about Davy Crockett that year. Inside was a sandwich wrapped in wax paper, and a little thermos of milk that was never quite cold enough by noon.
scenes.caption: THE METAL LUNCHBOX

scenes.text: Your classroom had tall windows and wooden desks in neat rows. Some still had an inkwell hole in the corner, left over from your parents' generation. At the front of the room hung an American flag, and a portrait of George Washington looking down at you very seriously.
scenes.caption: THE CLASSROOM

scenes.text: Every morning began the same way. You stood up, put your hand over your heart, and said the Pledge of Allegiance. Just the year before, in nineteen fifty-four, two new words had been added to it. Under God. Your older cousins had learned it one way. You learned it the new way.
scenes.caption: 1954: "UNDER GOD" ADDED

scenes.text: You learned to read with Dick and Jane. See Spot run. Run, Spot, run. You practiced penmanship over and over, the loops and curves of cursive writing, until your hand ached. The teacher was an authority you didn't question. And if you got in trouble at school, you got in trouble again at home.
scenes.caption: DICK AND JANE

scenes.text: At midmorning, a little carton of milk appeared on every desk, and you drank it through a paper straw. Every week, the Weekly Reader arrived, a thin newspaper just for kids, telling you about rockets and faraway countries and the wonders of the future. And four times a year, you carried home a report card in a stiff paper envelope, and handed it to your father, and waited.
scenes.caption: THE REPORT CARD

scenes.text: And then there were the drills. Every so often, without warning, the teacher would call out, and the whole class would drop to the floor and crawl under their desks, hands folded over the backs of their necks. Duck and cover. You'd seen the film, with Bert the Turtle, who pulled his head into his shell when danger came.
scenes.caption: DUCK AND COVER

scenes.text: You did it the way children do everything. Half seriously, half giggling. But somewhere deep down, a little seed of worry got planted. Your generation was among the first to grow up knowing the whole world could end on an ordinary Tuesday. You carried that, quietly, for a long time.
scenes.caption: A QUIET WORRY

scenes.text: At recess, though, the worry disappeared. There was kickball and tag and jump rope, and the girls chanting rhymes while the rope slapped the blacktop. There were marbles, and trading cards, and whoever was the fastest runner in the class. You always remember who that was, don't you? Even now.
scenes.caption: RECESS

scenes.text: When the last bell rang, you were free. You dropped your books at home, grabbed a cookie if your mother wasn't looking, and you were gone. There was one rule, really just one. Be home when the streetlights come on. Until then, the whole neighborhood belonged to you.
scenes.caption: HOME BY STREETLIGHTS
scenes.chapter: Out until the streetlights came on

scenes.text: And now, at last, that bicycle came into its own. Maybe it was a Schwinn, heavy and solid, with balloon tires and a chrome bell. You clipped a playing card to the fork with one of your mother's clothespins, so it clattered against the spokes and sounded, at least to you, exactly like a motorcycle.
scenes.caption: A CARD IN THE SPOKES

scenes.text: You learned to ride with no hands. You learned to skid in the gravel. You learned what it felt like to fall, get up, and not tell anybody about the scrape on your knee until dinner. That bicycle was freedom.
scenes.caption: NO HANDS

scenes.text: It took you to the creek, to the vacant lot, and to the corner store, where a bottle of Coca-Cola still cost about a nickel, and a candy bar cost about a nickel too. A comic book was a dime. If you found an empty soda bottle in a ditch, you could return it for a couple of cents. Kids in your neighborhood knew where every empty bottle in town was hiding.
scenes.caption: A NICKEL FOR A COKE

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty-five, it seemed like every boy in America wanted a coonskin cap. Walt Disney's Davy Crockett had been on television that winter, and suddenly the stores couldn't keep the caps on the shelves. Boys wore them in July. Boys wore them to bed. You sang the Davy Crockett song until your parents begged you to stop.
scenes.caption: THE DAVY CROCKETT CRAZE

scenes.text: You played cowboys with cap guns that smelled like burnt paper. You played army in the woods. You built forts out of old boards and blankets, and you made the rules, and you settled your own arguments, because there were no grown-ups around to settle them for you.
scenes.caption: COWBOYS AND CAP GUNS

scenes.text: The girls played house with baby dolls, and jacks on the front steps, and hopscotch drawn in chalk on the sidewalk. Everybody roller-skated on metal skates that clamped to your shoes and tightened with a key, a key you wore on a string around your neck.
scenes.caption: THE SKATE KEY

scenes.text: A few years later, the toys got even better. In nineteen fifty-eight, a company called Wham-O started selling a simple plastic ring called the Hula Hoop, and millions sold in just a few months. Then came the Frisbee. And then, in nineteen fifty-nine, a doll named Barbie.
scenes.caption: 1958: THE HULA HOOP

scenes.text: But in nineteen fifty-five, you didn't need much. You had a bicycle, a few friends, and a whole long afternoon. And when the sky turned orange, and then purple, and the first streetlight buzzed on at the end of the block, you heard your mother calling your name from the back porch. And you rode home, tired and dirty and happy, as fast as your legs would carry you.
scenes.caption: WHEN THE LIGHTS CAME ON

scenes.text: In the evenings, and on Saturday mornings, the television became your window on the world. There was Howdy Doody, with his freckles and his big grin, and Buffalo Bob, and the Peanut Gallery full of lucky kids sitting in the studio.
scenes.caption: HOWDY DOODY
scenes.chapter: What you watched and what you heard

scenes.text: Then, in October of nineteen fifty-five, something new arrived. A show called the Mickey Mouse Club. Kids all over the country put on felt hats with big round ears and sang along. You know the song. You can probably still hear it.
scenes.caption: OCTOBER 1955: MICKEY MOUSE CLUB

scenes.text: That very same week, a gentle man with a bowl haircut and a coat with enormous pockets appeared on C B S. His name was Captain Kangaroo. He would still be there, quietly, decades later, for your own children.
scenes.caption: CAPTAIN KANGAROO

scenes.text: Your parents watched I Love Lucy, and laughed until they cried. They watched Ed Sullivan on Sunday nights. And in September of nineteen fifty-five, a western called Gunsmoke came to television. It would run for twenty years.
scenes.caption: SEPTEMBER 1955: GUNSMOKE

scenes.text: On Sunday evenings, the whole family gathered for Lassie, the collie who always found the boy in time. And when the show ended, it was bath time, and bedtime, and the quiet feeling that a new school week was waiting on the other side of the night. You fell asleep listening to the murmur of your parents' television through the bedroom wall.
scenes.caption: SUNDAY NIGHT: LASSIE

scenes.text: On Saturday afternoons, there was the movie matinee. For a few coins you got a cartoon, a newsreel, a cliffhanger serial, and a feature, all in one long, loud, popcorn-scented afternoon. The theater was dark and cool, and the balcony was where the big kids sat.
scenes.caption: THE SATURDAY MATINEE

scenes.text: But the biggest change wasn't on the screen at all. It was on the radio. In the summer of nineteen fifty-five, a song called Rock Around the Clock, by Bill Haley and His Comets, climbed all the way to number one. Teenagers went wild for it. Some parents were horrified.
scenes.caption: 1955: ROCK AROUND THE CLOCK

scenes.text: It was loud, and it was fast, and it seemed to come from somewhere the grown-ups didn't understand. You were only seven, but you noticed. Your older cousins combed their hair differently. The big kids at the drugstore fed nickels into the jukebox.
scenes.caption: THE JUKEBOX

scenes.text: A few years later, the music went into your pocket. Small transistor radios, made of plastic and powered by a battery, let teenagers carry rock and roll anywhere. To the beach. To the backyard. Under the covers at night, with the volume turned way down so your parents wouldn't hear. For the first time, the music belonged to the kids.
scenes.caption: THE TRANSISTOR RADIO

scenes.text: And then, in September of nineteen fifty-six, a young man from Tupelo, Mississippi, with long sideburns and a curled lip, appeared on The Ed Sullivan Show. Elvis Presley. Around sixty million people watched, by the most common estimate. Your parents watched with their arms folded. And you watched with your mouth open.
scenes.caption: 1956: ELVIS ON ED SULLIVAN

scenes.text: The world was getting louder. And you were getting older.
scenes.caption: THE WORLD GOT LOUDER

scenes.text: Now let's talk about money. Because if you grew up in nineteen fifty-five, you've probably told your grandchildren about the prices, and they've probably looked at you like you made it all up. You didn't.
scenes.caption: WHAT THINGS COST

scenes.text: In the middle of the fifties, a gallon of gasoline cost somewhere around twenty-five cents, depending on where you lived. And a man in a uniform pumped it for you, washed your windshield, and checked your oil, without you ever leaving your seat.
scenes.caption: GAS: ~25 CENTS A GALLON

scenes.text: A loaf of bread was under a quarter. A first-class stamp was three cents. A movie ticket was well under a dollar, and kids got in for even less on Saturday afternoons.
scenes.caption: BREAD UNDER A QUARTER · STAMP 3¢

scenes.text: A brand-new Chevrolet, the beautiful nineteen fifty-five Bel Air with its new V eight engine, cost roughly two thousand dollars. And a new house in the suburbs cost around ten thousand dollars or more.
scenes.caption: 1955 BEL AIR: ~$2,000 NEW

scenes.text: But here's the part the grandchildren always forget. Money was smaller, too. According to the Census Bureau, the typical American family earned around four thousand, four hundred dollars a year in nineteen fifty-five. The federal minimum wage was seventy-five cents an hour, and it went up to a whole dollar the following spring.
scenes.caption: FAMILY INCOME ~$4,400 A YEAR

scenes.text: So when your father bought that Chevrolet, it was a very big decision, talked over at the kitchen table for weeks. People paid cash for most things. They saved up. A family might have one car, one television, and one telephone.
scenes.caption: ONE CAR, ONE TV, ONE PHONE

scenes.text: The telephone was mounted on the wall, or sat on a little table in the hallway, with a rotary dial that clicked back around after every number. And if you were unlucky, it was a party line, where the neighbors could pick up and listen in on your conversation. On a party line, everybody knew everybody's business.
scenes.caption: THE PARTY LINE

scenes.text: If you needed to call your grandmother in another state, it was an event. Long distance was expensive, so the whole family crowded around the phone, each person taking a turn, talking fast, and somebody always saying, hurry up, this is costing money. Most of the time, people simply wrote letters, and waited a week for the reply.
scenes.caption: LONG DISTANCE WAS AN EVENT

scenes.text: Your allowance might have been a quarter a week. Maybe fifty cents, if you mowed the lawn. And a quarter could buy you a comic book, a soda, a candy bar, and still leave a little change for the gumball machine.
scenes.caption: A QUARTER A WEEK

scenes.text: You didn't feel rich. Most families didn't. But you felt like things were getting better every single year. And for millions of American families in the nineteen fifties, they were.
scenes.caption: THINGS WERE GETTING BETTER

scenes.text: Some days in the year were different from all the others. Summer meant no school, and no shoes. By July, the bottoms of your feet were so tough you could run across hot pavement without flinching. You caught fireflies in a mason jar with holes punched in the lid, and set them free before bed. Or forgot, and felt terrible in the morning.
scenes.caption: SUMMER: NO SCHOOL, NO SHOES

scenes.text: You ran through the lawn sprinkler. You waited, every single afternoon, for the bell of the ice cream truck, and when you heard it three blocks away, the whole neighborhood came running.
scenes.caption: THE ICE CREAM TRUCK

scenes.text: On the Fourth of July, there was a parade down Main Street, with the high school band and the veterans marching in their old uniforms. There was a picnic, with potato salad and watermelon, and somebody's uncle in charge of the grill. And when it got dark, you sat on a blanket and watched the fireworks bloom over the ball field.
scenes.query: Fourth of July parade small town 1950s
scenes.caption: THE FOURTH OF JULY

scenes.text: Sundays were quieter. Most stores were closed. Many families went to church in their best clothes, the girls in white gloves and the boys in clip-on ties that pinched. Then came Sunday dinner, the biggest meal of the week, maybe a pot roast that had been cooking all morning.
scenes.caption: SUNDAY BEST

scenes.text: And in the afternoon, a drive. Just a drive. Your father would say, let's go for a ride, and the whole family would pile into the car and go nowhere in particular, just to look at the farms, or the new houses going up, or the lake.
scenes.caption: THE SUNDAY DRIVE

scenes.text: And then there was Christmas. The big department store catalog arrived in the fall, and you read it until the pages went soft, circling everything you wanted with a pencil. An electric train. A baby doll. A real air rifle, if your mother could be talked into it, which she usually couldn't.
scenes.caption: THE CHRISTMAS CATALOG

scenes.text: The tree was a real one, and the lights were big, hot, colored bulbs. If one bulb went out, sometimes the whole string went dark, and your father spent an hour testing every single one, grumbling under his breath. You threw the tinsel on in clumps, and your mother came behind you and fixed it, one strand at a time.
scenes.caption: THE CHRISTMAS TREE

scenes.text: On Christmas Eve, you could hardly sleep. And on Christmas morning, in your pajamas, in the gray light before dawn, you crept down the stairs and saw it. The tree lit up. The presents underneath. And for a moment, everything in the world was exactly the way it was supposed to be.
scenes.caption: CHRISTMAS MORNING

scenes.text: There's one thing about nineteen fifty-five that people who weren't there can never quite understand. Before that year, every summer, American parents were afraid. They were afraid of polio.
scenes.caption: THE FEAR OF POLIO
scenes.chapter: The year America stopped being afraid

scenes.text: Polio came in the warm months. It paralyzed thousands of children every year. Swimming pools closed. Parents kept their kids away from crowds, away from movie theaters, away from the beach. Some children ended up in leg braces. Some ended up in iron lungs, huge metal machines that breathed for them, lined up in hospital wards.
scenes.caption: IRON LUNGS

scenes.text: Every mother in America knew the fear of a child who woke up with a stiff neck and a fever. Then, on April twelfth, nineteen fifty-five, the news came over the radio. The vaccine developed by Doctor Jonas Salk was safe, and it worked.
scenes.caption: APRIL 12, 1955: THE SALK VACCINE WORKS

scenes.text: Church bells rang. People cried in the streets. And soon you were standing in a long line at school, or in the gymnasium, rolling up your sleeve, trying very hard to be brave, for a shot that meant you would never have to be afraid of polio again. A lot of kids remember that shot more clearly than almost anything else from that year. Maybe you do too.
scenes.caption: THE SHOT IN THE GYMNASIUM

scenes.text: That same summer, on July seventeenth, something else opened its gates out in California. A place called Disneyland. Most families couldn't go, not that year, and maybe not ever. But you saw it on television, and you dreamed about it, and for a whole generation of children, it felt like the future had arrived.
scenes.caption: JULY 17, 1955: DISNEYLAND OPENS

scenes.text: There were other things happening too, things a seven-year-old might not fully understand. In Des Plaines, Illinois, a salesman named Ray Kroc opened his first McDonald's restaurant that spring.
scenes.caption: 1955: RAY KROC'S FIRST McDONALD'S

scenes.text: And in December, in Montgomery, Alabama, a woman named Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a city bus. The grown-ups talked about that one in low voices at the dinner table. It would take you years to understand just how much that moment would change your country.
scenes.caption: DECEMBER 1955: ROSA PARKS

scenes.text: And then the years began to move faster. In nineteen fifty-six, President Eisenhower signed the law that created the Interstate Highway System. Soon your family was taking road trips on wide new roads, stopping at motels with swimming pools and neon signs.
scenes.caption: 1956: THE INTERSTATE HIGHWAYS

scenes.text: You sat in the back seat, with no seat belt, playing the license plate game, asking are we there yet, until your father threatened to turn the car around. And on summer nights you went to the drive-in in your pajamas, and fell asleep in the back seat before the second feature.
scenes.caption: THE DRIVE-IN

scenes.text: In October of nineteen fifty-seven, you were nine, and one evening your father took you out into the backyard and pointed up at the sky. Somewhere up there, a little silver ball called Sputnik was beeping its way around the Earth. The Soviets had put it there. And the grown-ups, who had seemed so sure of everything, suddenly looked worried.
scenes.caption: OCTOBER 1957: SPUTNIK

scenes.text: Within a year, your school was talking about science and mathematics like never before. The space race had begun, and you were right in the middle of it.
scenes.caption: THE SPACE RACE BEGINS

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty-nine, you were eleven, and a new decade was coming. Alaska and Hawaii became the forty-ninth and fiftieth states, and soon a new flag with fifty stars hung on the classroom wall. Your father's car grew enormous tail fins. Everything seemed to point toward the sky, and toward tomorrow.
scenes.caption: 1959: 50 STARS AND TAIL FINS

scenes.text: In nineteen sixty, you were twelve, and you watched a young senator named John F. Kennedy debate Richard Nixon on television. It was the first televised presidential debate. Kennedy won the election. He seemed so young. He made the future sound exciting.
scenes.caption: 1960: THE FIRST TV DEBATE

scenes.text: Your body was changing, and so was everything else. Junior high meant lockers and changing classes and the terrifying school dance, where the boys stood on one side of the gym and the girls stood on the other, and the chaperones watched from the door. Somebody finally crossed the floor. Maybe it was you.
scenes.caption: THE SCHOOL DANCE

scenes.text: In October of nineteen sixty-two, you were fourteen, and for thirteen long days, the whole country held its breath over missiles in Cuba. Those duck and cover drills suddenly didn't feel like a game anymore.
scenes.caption: OCTOBER 1962: 13 DAYS

scenes.text: And then came November twenty-second, nineteen sixty-three. You were fifteen. Almost everyone your age remembers exactly where they were. A teacher came into the room, or the principal's voice came over the loudspeaker, and you heard that the president had been shot in Dallas. School let out early.
scenes.caption: NOVEMBER 22, 1963

scenes.text: At home, the television stayed on for days. It was the first time many of you ever saw your father cry.
scenes.caption: THE TV STAYED ON FOR DAYS

scenes.text: But even in that dark winter, something bright was coming. On February ninth, nineteen sixty-four, four young men from Liverpool walked onto the stage of The Ed Sullivan Show. The Beatles. Around seventy-three million Americans watched that night.
scenes.caption: FEBRUARY 9, 1964: THE BEATLES

scenes.text: If you were fifteen or sixteen, you remember the screaming, and your parents shaking their heads, and the feeling deep in your chest that your generation finally had something of its own.
scenes.caption: SOMETHING OF YOUR OWN

scenes.text: And now we come to the end of our journey. Or really, to the beginning of a new one. When you turned sixteen, sometime around nineteen sixty-four, one thing mattered more than anything else in the world. Your driver's license.
scenes.caption: SIXTEEN: THE LICENSE

scenes.text: Maybe you took driver's education at school, in a car with an extra brake pedal on the passenger side for the instructor, who gripped the dashboard every time you turned a corner. Maybe your father taught you, out on an empty country road on a Sunday afternoon, telling you to watch the clutch, watch the clutch, watch the clutch.
scenes.caption: WATCH THE CLUTCH

scenes.text: You stalled it a dozen times. And then, one day, you didn't. And then came the car. Very few kids got a new one. In April of nineteen sixty-four, Ford introduced the Mustang, at a base price of about two thousand, three hundred sixty-eight dollars, and every teenager in America wanted one. But you probably didn't get a Mustang.
scenes.caption: APRIL 1964: THE MUSTANG

scenes.text: You got something used. Something with a few dents, and a radio that only pulled in two stations, and a smell of old cigarettes and motor oil that never quite went away. Maybe it was a fifty-five Chevy, the same model your father had been so proud of when you were seven. Now it was nine years old, and it was yours.
scenes.caption: A NINE-YEAR-OLD '55 CHEVY

scenes.text: You paid for it with money you saved yourself, from a paper route, or bagging groceries, or pumping gas at the corner station. Every dollar of it was yours, and that made the car feel like the most valuable thing in the world.
scenes.caption: PAID WITH YOUR OWN MONEY

scenes.text: The first time you drove alone, with nobody in the passenger seat, you went nowhere special. Maybe just around the block, and then around again. But you rolled the window down, and you felt the air on your arm, and you understood something that nobody had to explain to you. You were grown. Or close enough.
scenes.caption: YOUR FIRST DRIVE ALONE

scenes.text: You washed it every Saturday. You knew every rattle and every squeak. You drove your friends to the drive-in, and to the burger stand, and around and around Main Street on Friday night with the windows down and the radio up.
scenes.caption: FRIDAY NIGHT ON MAIN STREET

scenes.text: At the drive-in restaurant, a carhop came out to your window, sometimes on roller skates, and hung a tray right on the door. A burger, fries and a shake, and all your friends in the next car over, honking and laughing. Gas was still around thirty cents a gallon, so you could cruise all night on a couple of dollars.
scenes.caption: THE CARHOP

scenes.text: Maybe that car carried you to your first real date. You picked her up at her front door, and shook her father's hand, and promised to have her home by eleven. Maybe you kept that promise. Maybe you didn't. Either way, you remember that night.
scenes.caption: YOUR FIRST DATE

scenes.text: That car was freedom, just like the bicycle had been. Only now, the neighborhood wasn't big enough anymore. Now the road went all the way to the horizon.
scenes.caption: THE ROAD TO THE HORIZON

scenes.text: So that was the journey. From a red bicycle leaning against a porch in nineteen fifty-five, to a used car humming in the driveway nine years later. In those years, you went from Howdy Doody to the Beatles. From the milkman to the supermarket. From a world where polio terrified every parent, to a world where children rolled up their sleeves and the fear simply went away.
scenes.caption: FROM 1955 TO 1964

scenes.text: You hid under your desk, watched a satellite cross the night sky, and saw a president laid to rest. And through all of it, you grew up. The world you grew up in is gone now. The milkman doesn't come anymore. The screen doors don't slam the same way. Nobody calls the kids home when the streetlights come on.
scenes.caption: THAT WORLD IS GONE

scenes.text: But if you lived it, you carried it with you. Every bit of it. The smell of your mother's kitchen. The clatter of that playing card in the spokes. The sound of the engine the first time you turned the key. That world is still there. It's in you.
scenes.caption: IT'S STILL IN YOU

scenes.text: Now I'd love to hear from you. In the comments below, tell me what year you turned ten, and what your very first car was. I read every one of them, and some of your stories will become future videos on this channel.
scenes.caption: WHAT YEAR DID YOU TURN 10?

scenes.text: And if this brought back memories, you'll enjoy our next journey. Because if you turned eighteen in nineteen fifty-seven, your story is waiting for you, right here. Thank you for spending this time with me. Until next time, take care of yourself.
